title: Science never proved bumblebees cannot fly.
description:
Science never proved bumblebees cannot fly. The sums behind the story assumed a rigid, smooth wing, according to Snopes.

Wrote in Le Vol des Insectes that applying air resistance laws made insect flight impossible. The sums were by his assistant.

It treated a bee like a jumbo jet. Jumbo jets have fixed wings. The calculation only showed that bees with smooth, rigid wings cannot glide.

How often a bumblebee beats its wings on average, according to Science News.

Real wings bend and twist. Stroke angles change, and air flows over the wing in a way that creates lift. Snopes credits Torkel Weis-Fogh at Cambridge in the 1970s.

Nobody agrees who did the sums. Some accounts name students of Ludwig Prandtl, others Swiss gas dynamicist Jacob Ackeret. The 1934 book is the earliest known reference.

The bee was fine. The model was wrong.

Sources:
- https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/bumblebees-cant-fly/: read. Established that Magnan included a passage in the introduction to his 1934 book Le Vol des Insectes saying that applying the laws of air resistance to insects made their flight "impossible"; that the calculation was by his assistant, apparently an engineer; that the dinner anecdote is variously tied to students of Ludwig Prandtl or to Swiss gas dynamicist Jacob Ackeret; that the calculation assumed a rigid, smooth wing (bee of almost a gram, wing area about a square centimetre, per Physics World 1996); that wings are not rigid and bend and twist; and that Torkel Weis-Fogh, Cambridge zoologist in the 1970s, did the key work on how insect wings generate lift.
- https://www.sciencenews.org/article/flight-bumblebee: read. Established the same Magnan 1934 passage and dinner anecdote, "Wings aren't rigid", and the figure that a bumblebee beats its wings 130 times per second on average.
- https://www.todayifoundout.com/index.php/2013/08/bumblebee-flight-does-not-violate-the-laws-of-physics/: read (2013 blog post, secondary). Established that Le Vol des Insectes is the earliest known reference, and that the calculation fails because bumblebees do not fly like planes or have stiff rigid wings.
